2.  FISCAL YEAR 2024-25 APPROPRIATION LIMIT – F2M24-17, R2M24-21, M2M24-110

  Director of Finance LIEU delivered a staff report. Proposition XIII B (Gann Initiative) prohibited
  local agencies from exceeding their 1978-79 fiscal year appropriations after allowing for cost-
  of-living (CPI) and population changes which were certified by the State Department of
  Finance. Proposition 111 allowed the City to adjust its annual limits for the following factors,
  subject to approval by the City Council:

  a)  Either the California Per Capita Income or the percentage change in local assessment
  roll from the preceding year due to the addition of local nonresidential construction in
  the City.
  b)  Either the City’s own population growth or the population growth of the entire county.

  Government Code Section 7910 required agencies to adopt a resolution each year disclosing
  their appropriation limit. In accordance with Proposition 111, the City was required to conduct
  a review of their appropriations limit during the annual financial audit. For Fiscal Year 2022-
  2023, the City’s appropriation limit was reviewed by our auditors, Moss, Levy & Hartzheim,
  LLP, and determined to be properly calculated. The calculations in computing the City of
  Alhambra’s appropriation limit for the 2024-2025 fiscal year are on file in the Finance
  Department. The appropriation limit for the 2024-25 fiscal year was $189,333,947 and the
  applicable appropriation subject to this limitation is $82,639,781. Therefore, the City was
  favorably under the appropriations limit by $106,694,166.

  Opened & Closed the Public Hearing: Mayor PÉREZ opened the public hearing and as
  there was no one present who wished to speak, closed the same.

  2
6-24-24
   Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council adopted Resolution No. R2M24-21 entitled: A Resolution
  of the Alhambra City Council establishing the Appropriation Limit for FY 2024-25 and
  approving the annual adjustment factors used in the calculation thereof; and, approved the
  annual adjustment factors (per capita income change +3.62% and City population change
  +0.05%) used in the calculation of the appropriation limit. (M2M24-110)

  Vote:  Moved:  MALONEY  Seconded:  MAZA

3.  PUBLIC HEARING TO ADOPT ORDINANCE O2M24-4831 APPROVING ZONING TEXT
  AMENDMENT AMD-24-01 MAKING GENERAL CLARIFYING UPDATES TO THE CITY’S
  ZONING CODE AND DETERMINE THIS ACTION IS EXEMPT FROM CEQA – F2M20-24,
  N2M24-73, O2M24-4831

  This was the time and place set by Notice No. N2M24-73 for the City Council to hold a public
  hearing to consider an ordinance approving a Zone Text Amendment amending various
  sections of the Alhambra Municipal Code on zoning, as well as adding new sections, to
  address new State legislation and clarify ambiguous provisions as well as correct
  typographical and formatting errors and modify use allowances. Director of Community
  Development HO delivered a staff report and presentation, which is on file in the City Clerk’s
  office. At its February 26, 2024 meeting, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. O2M24-4828,
  which proposed minor changes to the AMC to reflect current practices, clarify confusing parts
  of the AMC, and bring outdated sections into compliance with State law. This ordinance was
  brought separately from Ordinance No. O2M24-4828 because it proposed changes to the
  City’s Zoning Code, which required review by the City’s Planning Commission. This proposed
  clean-up addressed items that were identified in the lead-up to and shortly after the January
  22, 2024 adoption and March 2, 2024 implementation of the comprehensive Zoning Code
  update, including addressing new State legislation, eliminating inconsistencies, and creating
  greater clarity in implementing the new Zoning Code. The various items being addressed in
  this Municipal Code clean-up fell within two (2) broad categories: 1) proposed amendments
  and 2) proposed additions. All of the proposed amendments and additions were reviewed for
  consistency with the City’s General Plan, as required by AMC Section 23.33.080 (General
  Plan Consistency Required for Zoning Amendments). In Attachment 1 of staff’s June 24, 2024
  report, each proposed amendment and addition was briefly described in a table, which
  included a breakdown of the categories applicable to each amendment or addition, as well as
  any recommended changes by the Planning Commission.

  At their May 6, 2024 regular meeting, the Planning Commission reviewed the proposed
  ordinance and adopted Planning Commission Resolution No. 24-09, recommending the City
  Council approve Zoning Text Amendment AMD-24-01 with four revisions to the proposed
  regulations for Personal Storage uses. Additionally, in response to Planning Commission
  questions regarding the meaning of “public projects” in the proposed new section 23.01.090,
  minor changes were made to the language of that section from what was presented to the
  Planning Commission to clarify the definition. Since being presented to the Planning
  Commission, a couple of additional non-substantive changes were made to the language in
  the ADU section, the sections relating to Community Development Director hearing
  procedures, and to the provisions related to minimum residential density requirements to
  further clarify these provisions.

  The City reviewed the environmental impacts of the proposed ordinance under the California
  3
6-24-24
   Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and the
  regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA
  Guidelines”). This Ordinance was not subject to further review environmental review because:
  (1) it would not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the
  environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15060(c)(2); (2) there was no possibility that this
  Ordinance would have a significant effect on the environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. §
  15061(b)(3)); and (3) the Ordinance, by itself, did not constitute a “project” as defined in section
  21065 of the Public Resources Code and the CEQA Guidelines (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15378).
  It could be seen with certainty that there was no possibility that this Ordinance would have a
  significant effect on the environment.

  Open Public Hearing: Mayor PÉREZ opened the public hearing.

  Public Comment:

  1) Robert TAM, 2424 Poplar Blvd., representing Caster Properties & Robert Tam, spoke
  regarding storage regulations as they relate to the A-1 Self Storage property.

  2) Brian CASTER, 4602 Mission Gorge Road, 92120, representing Caster Properties &
  Robert Tam, spoke regarding storage regulations as they relate to the A-1 Self Storage
  property. He also submitted his comments as a letter to the Planning Commission.

  3) John LA RAIA, 4602 Mission Gorge Road, 92120, representing Caster Properties & Robert
  Tam, spoke regarding storage regulations as they relate to the A-1 Self Storage property.
  He also submitted his comments as a letter to the Planning Commission.

  4) Lewis McCAMMON, 105 N. Cordova St., made comments regarding changes
  incorporated in order to satisfy the concerns of the California Department of Housing and
  Community Development with regards to the Housing element. He commented on the
  minimum residential density and mixed-use developments. He also submitted a handout
  to Council, which is on file in the City Clerk’s office.

  5) William Durslag, via Zoom, spoke as a commercial real estate broker and his experiences
  dealing with mixed use projects and self storage/mixed use retail projects. He offered
  suggestions to Council regarding the design of such projects.

  6) Melissa Michelson, via Zoom, expressed there did not appear to be a need for more
  storage facilities and suggested that more research be conducted as to proposed uses of
  the industrial zones. She also made suggestions for bike plans for industrial zones.

  Closed Public Hearing:  After receiving public comment, Mayor PÉREZ closed the public
  hearing.

  Discussion: Councilmember MALONEY thanked the Planning Commission and staff for
  their work and proposed a continuation of the Urgency Ordinance temporary moratorium on
  the construction of self-storage facilities until more detailed plans could be approved. He
  discussed the suggestion for 50% of the ground floor of storage facilities being set aside for
  other use with Mr. HO who explained a recommendation to use a calculation of the street
  frontage of a proposed development be set aside, rather than a percentage of total square
  footage. Mr. HO explained that this way, proposed properties would more effectively utilize
  space and Mr. MALONEY agreed that this would allow for some flexibility for use and address
  the concerns regarding vacant retail space. Mr. MALONEY and Mr. HO continued to discuss
  the benefits of calculating mixed used based on street frontage. Mr. HO stated that this could
  be included in the ordinance not as a regulation but as a negotiated element in the
  development agreement.
  4
6-24-24
   Mr. MALONEY went on to refer to the Planning Commission discussions regarding the location
  of storage facilities on major arterials. He suggested that the language be changed to state,
  “all industrial properties fronting major arterials would be appropriate for self-storage,” and
  added that other major arterials were not appropriate in the city.

  Mr. MALONEY motioned to approve the ordinance with the Planning Commission
  recommendations, include the suggested language regarding the percentage of street
  frontage for additional use, and include restrictions for development near certain major
  arterials.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER pointed out the numerous storage facilities in
  Alhambra and agreed that there was a need for guidelines. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER and
  Mr. HO discussed the potential for residential units on site of storage facilities. She thanked
  staff and the Planning Commission for their work and discussed the suggestion of 50% of
  square footage for community use. She discussed the need for developments to meet the
  City’s guidelines for sustainability. She seconded Mr. Maloney’s motion.

  Councilmember MAZA thanked staff and the need to update zoning codes. He also supported
  Mr. MALONEY’s motion and supported the calculation of street frontage square footage being
  set aside for community or retail use. He also suggested that due to the different location of
  each storage facility, that the calculation of additional use be applied to developments with a
  minimum of 1,500 square footage.

  Vice Mayor LEE supported Mr. Maloney’s motion and spoke to the need to carefully consider
  every piece of land for the community. She also supported Mr. Maloney’s request to extend
  the temporary moratorium. She went on to discuss the possibilities of public and semi-public
  use with Mr. HO.

  Mr. HO and Mr. MAZA discussed his suggestion of a minimum square footage to apply to
  non-storage spaces. Mr. HO stated that a minimum square footage would be included in the
  ordinance.

  Action Taken:  City Council:

  1. Conducted a public hearing to receive public testimony;

  2. Determined which of the Planning Commission’s recommendations to include as well as
  made additional recommendations regarding minimum square footage for street frontage
  used for non-storage units and limiting zoning on major arterial intersections, and;

  3. Directed the City Attorney to introduce and give first reading by title only, waiving further
  reading to the following ordinance entitled:

  Ordinance No. O2M24-4831: AN ORDINANCE OF THE ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  ADOPTING ZONING TEXT AMENDMENT AMD-24-01 AMENDING THE ALHAMBRA
  MUNICIPAL  CODE  TO  ADDRESS  NEW  STATE  LAWS,  ELIMINATE
  INCONSISTENCIES,  CLARIFY  AMBIGIOUS  PROVISIONS,  CORRECT
  TYPOGRAPHICAL AND FORMATTING ERRORS, AND MODIFY USE ALLOWANCES

  which ordinance shall return for a second reading and adoption at the next City Council
  meeting on July 22, 2024.

  Vote:  Moved:  MALONEY  Seconded:  ANDRADE-STADLER
  Ayes:  MALONEY, MAZA, LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ

4.  AUTHORIZE RFP: PROFESSIONAL MARKETING AND ADVERTISING SERVICES IN
  SUPPORT OF THE CITY’S ORGANIC RECYCLING COLLECTION AND FOOD RECOVERY
  PROGRAMS – F2M24-49, RFP2M24-11

  The City launched the “Alhambra Recycles” campaign in 2023, a comprehensive and
  multilingual outreach campaign to provide public information on SB 1383 requirements. On
  April 22, 2024, the City Council accepted a grant in the amount of $218,610.00 from the
  Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery (CalRecycle) under the SB 1383 Local
  Assistance Grant Program. Staff received approval from CalRecycle to use $60,000 in Local
  Assistance Grant funds to develop and implement a multi-media marketing and advertising
  plan to disseminate information on organic recycling and food recovery to greater
  communities. Staff sought to solicit proposals from qualified consultants with professional
  expertise and experience to provide the City with digital and print advertising; marketing
  services to reach Alhambra’s diverse community; and additional “Alhambra Recycles”
  campaign material.

  Discussion:  None

  Action Taken:  City Council authorized the distribution of Request for Proposals (RFP)
  to qualified consultants to provide professional marketing and advertising services in support
  of the City’s organic recycling collection and food recovery programs in accordance with SB
  1383; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize the Council’s action.

  Vote:  Moved:  MALONEY  Seconded:  ANDRADE-STADLER
  Ayes:  MALONEY, MAZA, LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE

5.  AUTHORIZE RFP: PROFESSIONAL ENGINEERING DESIGN SERVICES FOR THE FY
  2024-2025 SB1 STREET REHABILITATION PROJECT – F2M24-45, RFP2M24-12

  The Road Repair and Accountability Act of 2017 (SB1 BEALL) increased funding to local
  streets and roads. Funds were allocated from the Highway Users Tax Account through the
  Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation Account (RMRA). On May 13, 2024, the City Council
  adopted Resolution R2M24-16, which identified the FY 2024-2025 street rehabilitation projects
  that would be funded by SB1, the Road Repair and Accountability Act. Generally, this project
  was for public streets bound by Valley Boulevard, Fremont Avenue, the I-10 freeway in the
  City of Alhambra and the West City Limit. Staff requested engineering, design, and estimating
  services to support the execution of projects.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council authorized the distribution of a Request for Proposals
  (RFP) for Professional Engineering Design Services for Plans, Specifications and Cost
  Estimate for the FY 2024-2025 SB1 Street Rehabilitation Project, with proposals due no later
  than 12:00 p.m. on Monday, July 26, 2024; and, directed staff to undertake the steps
  necessary to finalize the Council’s action.

6.  AWARD CONTRACT: MEN'S RESTROOM REMODEL AT THE ALHAMBRA CITY YARD
  PUBLIC WORKS BUILDING – F2M20-66, N2M24-19, C2M24-40, M2M24-89

  On February 12, 2024, the City Council approved the distribution of a Notice Inviting Bids for
  the Men’s Restroom Remodel at the City Yard Public Works Building. On May 9, 2024, the
  City Clerk received four bids ranging from $152,200 (Sanz Construction) to $270,500 (ENL
  Building Service Inc.). The bid received from Sanz Construction Inc. in the amount of $152,200
  was the lowest responsible bid, was in full compliance, and conformed with the bid
  specifications.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract, subject to final language approval by
  the City Manager and City Attorney, to Sanz Construction Inc. for the Men’s Restroom
  Remodel at the Alhambra City Yard in the amount not to exceed $152,200; found the project
  was categorically exempt from California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Section 15301(b)
  – existing facilities of both investor and publicly-owned utilities used to provide electric power,
  natural gas, sewerage, or other publicly utility services; and, directed staff to undertake the
  steps necessary to finalize Council’s action. (M2M24-89)

  Vote:  Moved:  MALONEY  Seconded:  ANDRADE-STADLER

7.  AWARD CONTRACT: CITY HALL LOBBY ATTENDANT SERVICES – F2M20-43,
  RFP2M24-7, C2M24-41, M2M24-90

  On April 8, 2024, staff sought Council authorization to solicit proposals for the City Hall Lobby
  Attendant Services. Proposals were due on May 6, 2024 and twenty proposals were received.
  A review committee comprised of three staff members reviewed the proposals. Staff
  evaluated the proposals based on professional and technical experience, experience providing
  similar services, understanding of City objectives and requirements, and hourly rates and
  administrative costs. Proposals were also reviewed for responsiveness on the required
  submittals. Good Guard Security, Inc. (Good Guard) was selected as the most qualified firm.
  Good Guard’s municipal contracts include The Altadena Public Libraries and cities of Los
  Angeles, Santa Monica, and Anaheim. A reference check was conducted and was satisfactory.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract, subject to final language approval by
  the City Manager and City Attorney, to Good Guard Security, Inc. for City Hall Lobby Attendant
  Services for a two-year contract not to exceed $55,186.56 in year one and not to exceed
  $57,101.12 in year two; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize the
  Council’s action. (M2M24-90)

  for the Construction and Construction Inspection Services for the Pedestrian Countdown

  On March 21, 2024, the City Clerk received three proposals. Staff reviewed and evaluated the
  responding proposals and found the proposal submitted by Z&K Consultants, Inc. conformed
  to the RFP and received the highest rating based on the following scoring factors:
  completeness of the proposal and compliance with the required RFP format, project
  understanding, scope and approach to develop the project efficiently, experience and
  qualifications of key staff, similar project experience, including familiarity with State and
  Federal procedures and Effectiveness of project schedule. Z&K Consultants, Inc. has served

21.  RESOLUTION DECLARING A PORTION OF CITY OWNED PROPERTY UPON WHICH THE
  WEST SAN GABRIEL VALLEY YMCA EXISTS AS EXEMPT SURPLUS LAND;
  APPROVING AN AGREEMENT TERMINATING CONCESSION AND TRANSFERRING
  PROPERTY TO ACCOMMODATE CONSTRUCTION OF A DOG PARK; DETERMINING
  THE TRANSFER OF PROPERTY AND CONSTRUCTION OF A DOG PARK IS EXEMPT
  FROM CEQA – F2M11-36, F2M18-35, R2M24-26, RFP2M24-13, M2M24-103

  The City of Alhambra was the fee owner of the property located at 401 Corto Street, Alhambra,
  California 91801, APN 5347-028-904 (the “Property”). The City and the West San Gabriel
  Valley YMCA entered into a concession agreement (the “Agreement”) in 1988 to allow the
  YMCA to construct and operate a YMCA recreational facility open to the general public. The
  YMCA subsequently constructed and has since operated such a facility on the western portion
  of the Property. The eastern portion of the Property was improved with a small below-grade
  parking area that was not currently used by the YMCA. The City now wished to construct a
  dog park on the eastern portion of the Property. That location was particularly suited for such
  a use as it was surrounded by the YMCA building to the West, a lowered railroad right of way
  to the North, a golf course driving range to the East and a large public parking lot to the South.
  The City also had funding for such a park—but the funding must be utilized in the next year.
  Due to the exclusive use rights held by the YMCA by virtue of the Agreement, the City was not
  able to utilize the eastern portion of the Property for a dog park. The YMCA was willing to
  terminate the Agreement, but wished to remain in operation. Accordingly, the YMCA would
  terminate the Agreement and relinquish any and all interest in the eastern portion of the
  Property in exchange for the City transferring the western portion of the Property to the YMCA,
  along with a one-time payment of $203,810. The payment was intended to compensate the
  15
6-24-24
   YMCA for the value of the loss of the eastern portion of the property (which they had the use
  of through 2083 under the Concession Agreement). The transferred property would be subject
  to a use covenant—the same covenant that existed in the current Agreement, limiting the use
  to a recreational facility open to the general public. Government Code Section 54221(f)(1)(C)
  allowed a City to transfer property as exempt surplus land, without offering the property to
  housing developers or recreational entities, when the property was being exchanged for City
  purposes. Exchanging the fee interest in the western portion of the site for a release of the
  lease rights held by the YMCA would allow the City to construct the public dog park. Without
  this exchange, the City would not have access to the Property until the end of the term of the
  Agreement. The proposed resolution would satisfy the requirements of the Government Code
  concerning transfers of public land. The transfer must also be approved by the California
  Department of Housing and Community Development. During the pendency of that approval,
  City staff requested authority to release a request for proposals for design services for the dog
  park so as not to lose time in furthering the project.

26.  ACCEPTANCE OF A GRANT FROM THE UNITED STATES BUREAU OF RECLAMATION
  UNDER THE WATERSMART SMALL-SCALE WATER EFFICIENCY GRANT PROGRAM –
  F2M24-18, M2M24-108

  On January 8, 2024, City Council approved Resolution No. R2M24-1 enabling the submittal of
  a grant application to the United States Bureau of Reclamation’s WaterSMART Grant Program
  for small-scale water efficiency projects that seek to conserve and better manage water
  supplies. On May 23, 2024, staff was notified that the City was selected to receive a grant of
  $100,000 under the WaterSMART Small-Scale Water Efficiency Grant Program. The project
  would replace approximately 458 water meters with Advanced Meter Infrastructure (AMI)
  equipment at various locations in the City and purchase an online customer portal software
  program. As required by the grant program, the City would contribute $111,115 in matching
  funds towards the project, which shall be covered by the Water Fund (Fund 401). The grant
  project advanced the citywide, multi-year water meter replacement program identified in the
  Capital Improvement Plan.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council accepted a grant in amount of $100,000 from the United
  States Bureau of Reclamation under the WaterSMART Small-Scale Water Efficiency Grant
  Program; appropriated revenue and expenditure funds; authorized the City Manager, or
  designee, to execute all documents related to grant implementation; and, directed staff to
  undertake the steps necessary to finalize the Council’s action. (M2M24-108)
